name: Anarch Territory, Feeding and Gang Structure

text.content: Anarch communities range from a single coterie squatting at the edge of a @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla}- or @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.6868ee8c357f4b73]{Sabbat}-held city to entire metropolitan areas under full anarch control. Unlike Camarilla princedoms or Sabbat dioceses, anarch authority is never institutional by default - it is granted by, and depends entirely on, the ongoing consent of the community. An anarch "officer," even a baron, holds power only so long as the community respects her judgment; the moment she loses that trust, her authority evaporates, formal title or not.

Anarchs feed the same way any other vampire does - as predators, thieves, seducers or via herds and animals - but unlike @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla} loyalists they rarely have any elder's permission to feed where they do, which makes them poachers by definition on whatever domain they hunt. The central feeding concern for most anarchs isn't how to feed, but knowing whose territory they're poaching on, how to avoid getting caught, and how that elder is likely to react when (not if) they're caught.

Consequences for poaching vary widely. Most of the time an elder simply extorts some minor service from the offender and lets the matter drop - it's rarely worth the trouble to make an example of a low-level upstart. Repeat offenders, or anarchs who pick the wrong night in the wrong part of town, can find themselves dragged before the prince with an elder demanding their head. This constant low-grade legal jeopardy is a major driver of anarch demands for equitable distribution of a city's feeding grounds: vampires who are denied blood long enough will frenzy, so anarchs argue they are made into criminals by necessity, not choice.

pages.name: The Blood Bond and Ghouls, Anarch-Style

text.content:
Anarchs revile the Blood Bond more consistently than any other issue in the Movement, to the point of using a distinct vocabulary for it: a regnant is called a Blood Slaver (a criminal to be punished) and a thrall a Blood Slave (a victim to be liberated). In most anarch communities, Blood Slavery is treated as a capital offense. The Bond is considered so heinous that anarchs sentenced to it by an elder will often flee to the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.6868ee8c357f4b73]{Sabbat} rather than submit, hoping (usually in vain) to escape once it fades. That said, hypocrisy runs deep: many anarchs quietly accept mutual Bonds between lovers, or excuse Bonding someone outside the Movement, their faction or their gang as "unfortunate but necessary." Mercenaries and Nihilists in particular will Bond others without qualm while working hard to avoid being Bound themselves, which is a major source of their unpopularity.

Ghouls present a similar contradiction: idealists who condemn Blood Slavery among vampires often keep ghoul retainers anyway, since a bond is difficult to avoid when maintaining loyal servants. Anarch ghouls are, in practice, usually treated better than their @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla} counterparts - many anarchs maintain a standing pledge to Embrace a mortally wounded retainer (or let them die naturally if preferred) and to stand by their ghouls in a crisis.

How anarchs organize a territory depends heavily on how contested that territory is.

Enemy Territory

Where the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla}, @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.6868ee8c357f4b73]{Sabbat} or another power fully dominates a city, anarchs are few, scattered and largely unorganized beyond sharing meager hunting grounds - open organizing invites destruction. Those who stay despite having means to leave are either unmotivated posers (who eventually drop out or defect) or disciplined guerrillas running covert cells that smuggle arms, allies and information under the enemy's nose. Such cells recognize no leader beyond their own cell heads and often avoid contact with other local anarchs to limit what a captured member could reveal under torture or mind-rape. Rumors of a single charismatic revolutionary leader in these territories are frequently anarch-planted disinformation meant to waste enemy resources chasing a decoy.

Disputed Territories

Where neither major sect fully controls a city, anarchs are more numerous and active, and typically defer to whichever local leader is most charismatic, backed by a handful of trusted lieutenants who liaise with outside groups. Formal councils are rare in disputed territory - a single decisive leader is usually more useful in an ongoing conflict than a divided body - though a council may form if a leader is deposed and no obvious successor emerges. Rival leaders and factions vying for the same ground can produce bitter rivalries, but outright Final Death between rival anarchs is rare and severely punished, since disputed territories are usually too weak to survive both external threats and internal bloodletting.

Anarch Territories

Where anarchs are the dominant power, organization scales with community size and civic-mindedness. Anarchs generally distrust vesting lasting, consolidated authority in a single vampire, fearing it invites tyranny; smaller communities may still follow a single baron as "first among equals," but larger communities generally prefer some form of council, evolving from informal ad hoc panels into more formal bodies as the population grows. Council composition can take almost any form (elected republic, council of elders, even lottery), but by convention all councils reserve at least one seat for each distinct gang or faction present (never allocated by clan, which anarchs view as reactionary). Some radicals reject any concentration of power at all, governing instead through popular assemblies open to all residents - a structure that's resistant to targeted decapitation but slow and vulnerable to coordinated sect interference. Across all forms, Anarch Free Territories are marked by an unusual degree of personal liberty: residents who keep the Masquerade and stay out of each other's business may come and go, hunt and sire largely as they please.

Anarch leaders derive all their authority from the consent of the community they lead, unlike a @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla} prince (absolute authority within his domain) or a @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.6868ee8c357f4b73]{Sabbat} archbishop (authority delegated downward from a cardinal). Anarch power is correspondingly broad in scope but weak in enforcement, resting on personal standing rather than institutional backing.

Baron

A community led by a single anarch, or a council that elevates one member to represent it, calls that vampire a baron - first among equals, deferred to because the community believes her the best available choice to avoid leading them to ruin. A baron's central job is dispute resolution between rival anarchs or gangs; her power rests almost entirely on personal magnetism and standing, and she must tread carefully between exercising real authority and appearing to set herself up as a petty tyrant. An unpopular decision can stick if her standing and charisma are strong enough - otherwise the community simply stops listening and finds a new baron.

Councilor

Where a community is led by a council instead, its members are called councilors. A councilor performs largely the same duties as a baron for the gang or faction she represents, but shares authority rather than holding it alone. Councils are common in larger communities that can't agree on a single leader, or that distrust vesting total authority in one person. They face less resistance implementing unpopular decisions (seen as less arbitrary than one person's fiat) but can deadlock over controversial issues, and councilor resignations in protest are common. Councils seat members by peer group/gang, not by clan - clan-based seating is considered reactionary, evoking Camarilla primogen councils.

Barons and councilors rely on assistants who hold no formal titles - only nicknames describing their function - and who, like their superiors, have only as much authority as they can personally command.

  • Ambassadors (also diplomats or emissaries) represent the community to other sects and independent clans, meeting with princes, primogen or bishops to persuade them to help or at least ignore the anarchs. The job's grim nickname is "expendable."
  • Counters (also monitors or sweepers) track who is coming and going from the community's territory, since demanding that fellow anarchs formally check in would be laughed out of practice.
  • Deputies (also sentinels or the militia) are volunteers who defend the territory, intervene in inter-gang conflict and apply force at council direction; larger communities try to draw deputies from every gang present to avoid accusations of favoritism.
  • Moles (also called Bonds) infiltrate enemy territory to gather intelligence, chiefly warning of impending @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla} or @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.6868ee8c357f4b73]{Sabbat} attacks and passing along useful information such as a vulnerable elder or an upcoming scourge sweep.

The gang is the anarchs' most common social unit, patterned loosely on modern urban street gangs. Gangs serve two purposes: physical security (a lone anarch is easy prey, but attacking her means risking a costly retaliatory war with her whole gang, and members often wear colors specifically to advertise this) and emotional support, since vampiric unlife - anarch unlife especially - is lonely, and gang bonds can reach a level of genuine devotion.

Gang Size and Territory

  • Small/urban gangs - five to seven members, one or two acting as leader. Rarely hold more than a single neighborhood unless unusually powerful or ghoul-heavy; weaker small gangs typically "squat" on a larger gang's turf (often paying tribute) or ally with peers to balance power.
  • Larger gangs - seven to fifteen members, subdivided into two or three "sets," each with its own set leader acting as lieutenant to the overall gang leader. Control two or three neighborhoods; the gang leader's headquarters sits in the largest. Formed either by rapid recruitment of a small gang or by several small, ideologically similar gangs merging into a "family," each becoming a set of the new whole.
  • Largest gangs - more than fifteen members across several sets, each set controlling an adjacent or strategically vital home neighborhood, collectively forming a single territorial claim (often an entire city ward). In the rare case a gang dominates an entire city and holds turf in neighboring cities as well, its leader becomes a "general," with a "captain" running each satellite city's turf through his own set lieutenants, and at least one set serving as a traveling "courier" group between cities.

Nomadic Gangs

Nomadic gangs pattern themselves on mortal biker clubs, lack (or don't want) fixed turf, and travel in caravans of trucks, vans and RVs, keeping arms and information moving between cities. They break into smaller sets than settled gangs to avoid drawing mortal attention, and individual sets enjoy more autonomy given how much time they spend apart from the whole; most hold periodic gatherings to trade news and supplies.

Guerrilla Units and Terrorist Cells

Guerrilla units operate entirely underground in independent cells, each member knowing only her immediate superior and cellmates, with all inter-cell communication coded or otherwise hard to trace. They claim no turf, maintain and readily abandon hidden training camps, and strike only when victory is effectively assured, favoring sudden decapitating strikes against a prince or archbishop's retinue followed by disappearance. Secrecy is absolute - membership and stronghold locations are fanatically guarded, and cell leadership readily sacrifices a compromised cell to protect the rest.

Joining an anarch gang follows a fairly standard, if lengthy, progression regardless of gang type.

  • Getting in: A hopeful must first prove genuine commitment to the Cause and the specific gang's agenda before the gang initiates a series of formal or informal tests - committing crimes, hitting a target (e.g., raising money) for urban gangs; enduring a grueling itinerary for nomadic gangs; demonstrating ideological knowledge and pulling off a daring, clean act of insurrection for guerrilla units. Candidates also typically face deliberate harassment, humiliation or even violence meant to test resolve.
  • Prospect: After passing initial tests and a final round of loaded questions, a candidate becomes a prospect, attached to the set controlling her neighborhood, and assigned a sponsor (almost a second sire) who vouches for her, defends her mistakes, and guides her through a probationary period of missions and gang integration.
  • Cousin: Once every gang member accepts the prospect as an equal, she becomes a cousin - bound to gang ideals and her set leader's orders, obligated to teach any Discipline she knows that the set lacks, and free to join debates but not to vote or challenge for leadership. Her sponsor delivers "indoctrination": instruction in the gang's structure, history, customs, ideology and territory.
  • Initiation: When her sponsor is satisfied, the set leader and gang leader arrange an initiation ordeal of severe physical and psychological tests (occasionally fatal) meant to expose disqualifying weaknesses. The candidate is offered at least three chances to withdraw without penalty (aside from a vow of silence or selective mindwipe). If she completes the ordeal, she swears a loyalty oath and receives her colors. Guerrilla units handle this very differently: a prospect never meets fellow cell members until she takes the loyalty oath (administered by the cell leader in the name of the central committee), and cell membership can take years or decades to earn.
  • Full membership: A fully initiated member gains any Discipline instruction the gang can offer, full voting and leadership-challenge rights, and the right to sponsor future prospects; she is oathbound to kill or die for her gang family and is addressed as "brother" or "sister" by fellow initiates only.
  • Getting out: Members who break under pressure and cost the gang a battle are usually branded cowards and expelled, or in worse cases executed if they know too much. Willful betrayal always earns a hunted, brutal death. Members who simply lose their passion for gang life are typically allowed to leave in peace, provided they keep gang secrets and don't join a rival gang or a sect.

vtmlarp.source: MET Mind's Eye Theatre Anarchs Guide
